artworks.title: The Flaying of Marsyas
artworks.description: Titian's late masterpiece in the Archdiocesan Museum at Kroměříž: Apollo and his assistants flay the defeated satyr Marsyas, hung upside down like a hunter's quarry. The thick, almost dissolving paint makes pain and music inseparable — one of the most unflinching images of divine punishment in Western art.

artworks.title: Apollo Flaying Marsyas
artworks.description: An oil by Jusepe de Ribera in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels. Apollo, luminous and calm, peels the skin from Marsyas in a shaft of light — Spanish tenebrism turned on the Phrygian contest's aftermath, the satyr's scream answering the god's pitiless clarity.

artworks.title: Athena and Marsyas
artworks.year: Roman copy after a Greek bronze of c. 450 BC
artworks.description: A Roman marble group after Myron's lost bronze: Athena has just discarded the aulos; Marsyas starts forward to claim the pipes she cursed. The moment before hubris — the satyr's first step toward the contest with Apollo — frozen in Classical restraint rather than in the later flaying.

artworks.title: The Flaying of Marsyas
artworks.description: An early oil by Agnolo Bronzino in the Hermitage, Saint Petersburg. Apollo and Marsyas face one another in the musical contest that will end in the satyr's flaying — Florentine Mannerism staging the Phrygian challenge as poised, almost courtly confrontation before the knife.

artworks.title: Apollo and Marsyas
artworks.description: A small panel in the Louvre long read as Apollo with the shepherd Daphnis and now often identified with the Marsyas contest: the god seated with his lyre opposite a youthful piper. Perugino's Umbrian calm turns the deadly rivalry into a quiet pastoral exchange — music before the flaying.

popCulture.title: Marsyas
popCulture.description: The satyr flayed for losing to Apollo remains art's most visceral image of hubris punished — Titian's knife and the hanging skin.
